sections.title: The big picture
sections.lede: Precision at C2 means choosing the word that is not only correct but right for the context.

blocks.text: Near-synonyms differ in connotation, intensity and collocation. “Günstig” is neutral or positive (good value), while “billig” can suggest low quality. “Zurückhaltend” is reserved or restrained; “gleichgültig” is indifferent. A single wrong choice can shift the whole tone.

Collocation is the company a word keeps: man trifft eine Entscheidung, man macht keinen Fehler (but: einen Fehler machen). “Irreführend” means misleading; “treffend” means apt or fitting. Learn these words with the nouns and verbs they naturally pair with.

blocks.title: Correct is not the same as right
blocks.text: A sentence can be grammatically correct and still sound wrong because a word carries the wrong connotation. Precision is the final layer of fluency.

sections.title: Rules & patterns
sections.lede: The patterns to keep in mind while you work through the examples.

rows: Das Wort „billig“ hat oft eine negative Konnotation.
Es heißt eine Entscheidung treffen, nicht eine Entscheidung machen.
Der Begriff ist in diesem Zusammenhang irreführend.

items: “Konnotation” is the feeling a word carries; “Denotation” is its literal meaning.
“Treffend” means precise and fitting: ein treffendes Beispiel.

sections.title: Pronunciation
sections.lede: Short, focused sound work. Play each item and repeat it twice.

blocks.text: German business and academic writing rewards precise word choice. A text that uses the same vague verb for every action (“machen”, “tun”) reads as unprofessional.
Connotation can differ between German-speaking regions. “Servus” is friendly in Austria and Bavaria but unusual in northern Germany. Context matters more than the dictionary.

sections.title: Speaking
sections.lede: Record or say your answer aloud, then compare it with the model.
sections.prompt: Explain the difference between two near-synonyms and correct one unnatural collocation.

model.de: „Günstig“ und „billig“ bedeuten beide wenig Geld, aber „billig“ hat oft eine negative Konnotation. Es heißt eine Entscheidung treffen, nicht eine Entscheidung machen. Der Begriff „billig“ ist in einem Werbetext daher irreführend.
model.en: “Günstig” and “billig” both mean little money, but “billig” often has a negative connotation. The correct phrase is to “treffen” a decision, not to “machen” a decision. The term “billig” is therefore misleading in an advertising text.

tips: Name the connotation, not just the literal meaning.
Give the correct collocation as a full phrase.
Explain why the wrong word would mislead the reader.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.lede: These are the errors learners most often make with this pattern.

items.why: The fixed collocation is eine Entscheidung treffen.

items.wrong: Der Begriff ist in diesem Zusammenhang irregeführt.
items.right: Der Begriff ist in diesem Zusammenhang irreführend.
items.why: The adjective is irreführend; irregeführt is the participle of irre führen.

items.wrong: Das treffend Wort ist hier Zurückhaltung.
items.right: Das treffende Wort ist hier Zurückhaltung.
items.why: The adjective before a noun needs an ending: das treffende Wort.
